title: Four Ministers Pledge a Coordination Center in the Philippines. One by That Name Already Exists
dek: The Oct. 28 commitment to establish a Combined Coordination Center follows two years in which the United States and the Philippines built and exercised a center under that name. No government has said whether the four-country body is that center, a wider version of it or something new.

body_paragraphs.text: The defense ministers of Australia, Japan, the Philippines and the United States have committed to “establishing a Combined Coordination Center (CCC) in the Philippines.” The commitment appears in a
joint statement
on their Oct. 28 meeting in Cebu, held on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus. Australia’s defence ministers posted it on Nov. 10, and Japan’s Ministry of Defense published the
Japanese text
the same day, listing the item as the establishment, or 設置, of the center. Neither version says where the center will be, how it will be organized or when it will open.

The center heads a list of four initiatives. The others are synchronizing defense investments to help the Philippines defend its archipelago, strengthening ministerial and senior policy consultations, and expanding the scope, complexity and frequency of combined exercises. The statement presents them as building on the recently signed Terms of Reference of the four countries’ Pacific Chiefs of Defense Cooperation Council (DCC) and on exercises such as Balikatan and Keen Sword. The Philippine Department of National Defense (DND) released the statement on Nov. 10 and gave no further details on the center’s location, structure, timeline or functions,
Manila Bulletin reported
The center did not appear in Japan’s account on the day of the meeting. The Ministry of Defense’s
readout
recorded Defense Minister Koizumi Shinjiro’s proposal to strengthen policy consultations, and his
news conference
that night noted that the DCC had been set up since the ministers last met. Neither the readout nor his opening remarks mentioned a coordination center. Nor did the
readout of their previous meeting
, in Kuala Lumpur in November 2025, which discussed information sharing and operational coordination and backed the framework for the DCC.
The name has a bilateral history. A
U.S. military account of Balikatan 25

in May 2025 described that year’s command post exercise as building on “the previous iteration’s Combined Coordination Center,” used in Balikatan 24 to synchronize separate Philippine and U.S. joint task forces. On that account, a U.S.–Philippine CCC existed as an exercise arrangement in 2024, months before the groundbreaking described below.
In November 2024, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III and Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr.
broke ground

on a new combined coordination center at Camp Aguinaldo, the headquarters of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) in Quezon City, on the visit in which they signed a bilateral General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA). A Pentagon
fact sheet
said the center would improve bilateral operational planning and let U.S. and Philippine forces work side by side in response to real-time incidents, “including those in the South China Sea.”
During Balikatan 25, a
U.S. exercise report

called the CCC at Camp Aguinaldo “a secure, joint operations node” where planners from both countries aligned the work of parallel U.S. and Philippine joint task forces. By the close of Balikatan 2026 the arrangement had become multinational. Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (INDOPACOM), said on May 8 that the entire multinational force had “embedded this structure, including the newly inaugurated Combined Coordination Center,” according to the
Indo-Pacific Defense Forum
, which INDOPACOM sponsors. The Forum placed that center at Camp Aguinaldo and described it as a hub between the AFP and INDOPACOM for multinational coordination.
Other accounts suggest more than one site.
USNI News reported

that the network ran from new combined coordination centers throughout the Philippines, funded by the United States through programs including the Pacific Deterrence Initiative and staffed by combined American and Filipino teams. Japan sent about 1,400 troops in its first Balikatan as a participant, and
INDOPACOM listed
Australia among the exercise’s participating countries.
This week’s accounts disagree on whether the four-country center exists yet. The joint statement speaks of establishing it, and
Manila Standard
described it on Nov. 12 as still planned. Teodoro, asked about the center on Nov. 11, said a coordination mechanism was coming and added, “Right now, it is already operating,”
GMA News reported
. He said locations could be disclosed once the parties agreed. GMA’s own summary of the interview placed the center in Manila, a location his quoted words did not give. The
Inquirer
noted that he did not say whether the mechanism was the facility used in Balikatan or a separate arrangement.

Teodoro spoke of a mechanism, not of the CCC by name. Three readings fit the record. The four-country CCC could be the Camp Aguinaldo center placed under a four-party arrangement; it could be a set of sites, consistent with the plural in the U.S. accounts and Teodoro’s reference to locations; or it could be a separate body that reuses a familiar name. As of Nov. 13, no government had said publicly which of these it is.

Japan’s public record shows a gap between the meeting and the statement. On Oct. 28 Koizumi described the four-way meeting, which he called the “SQUAD,” as the first in which all three of Japan’s partners there hold acquisition and cross-servicing agreements with Japan, and did not mention a center. Thirteen days later his ministry published the statement that lists the center first. The documents show that Japan accepted the language. They do not show what role, if any, the Self-Defense Forces would have in the center.

The statement’s word is coordination, and the Balikatan record shows what that has meant so far: a structure in which each side kept its own joint task force and the CCC kept them aligned. Paparo’s language in May went further. He said future Balikatan exercises would be led from there, which the Forum identified as Camp Aguinaldo, “through coalition combined command centers.” The ministers’ statement does not use command language.

The legal basis for sharing information is uneven across the four. The United States and the Philippines have had a GSOMIA since 2024. Japan and the Philippines do not yet have one; on Oct. 28 Koizumi said he and Teodoro had confirmed they would cooperate toward concluding one. In Balikatan 2026, multinational data sharing ran through a U.S. system:
INDOPACOM said

its common operating picture was open to eight nations, with foreign disclosure officers helping tag data so it could cross between networks. That design lets one U.S. network serve partners with different levels of access. The public record does not show a four-way framework for classified information, and these sources do not address arrangements between Australia and the Philippines.

The DCC Terms of Reference, signed by the four military chiefs in Singapore on May 29, cover information sharing, multilateral maritime activities, coordinated strategic communications, and interoperability in planning, logistics and sustainment,
according to Manila Bulletin
. The sources reviewed here do not include the text itself, so how a CCC would sit under it is unknown.

Four disclosures would settle the main question: where the center or centers are; whether Japanese and Australian officers are posted to them, and in what role; whether the center operates under the DCC Terms of Reference or a new instrument; and whether Japan and the Philippines conclude the information-security agreement Koizumi described. Until then, the record supports a narrower finding than the statement invites. Four governments have adopted as a shared goal a name that the United States and the Philippines have used for a bilateral coordination structure since at least 2024.
